items.title: HbA1c trial
items.intro: Five patients joined our diabetes education pilot. Here is their HbA1c, in %, before and after. Help me read the change.

recap.title: Change worked out
recap.subtitle: Five changes, an average fall of 0.64 points, and the percentage change per patient.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: How many patients are in the trial?
questions.explanation_after_check: c() combines the five results into one vector, and length() counts them: 5.
questions.takeaway: So: one vector holds every patient.

code_note.title: Vectors
code_note.text: `c()` combines values into one vector.

science_note.title: HbA1c
science_note.text: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over about 3 months, so trials measure it before and after an intervention.

questions.scene_label: Five patient cards with their starting HbA1c.

picture.description: Bars grow one after another against an optional reference line; value labels and a result note.
picture.label: HbA1c before the trial, per patient

options.feedback: That is the sum of the results.
before is one vector holding five values.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Work out each change
questions.explanation_after_check: R subtracts position by position: 7.5 − 8.4, 8.1 − 7.9, and so on. Negative means HbA1c fell.
questions.takeaway: So: change = after − before, per patient.
questions.hint_before_check: The change is after minus before.

code_note.title: Arithmetic on vectors
code_note.text: Arithmetic between two vectors pairs up their values.

science_note.title: Reading the change
science_note.text: A fall of 0.5 points or more is often treated as clinically meaningful for HbA1c.

questions.scene_label: Each card's after bar, ready to move.

picture.description: Bars grow one after another against an optional reference line; value labels and a result note.
picture.label: HbA1c after the trial, per patient

options.feedback: That adds them: about 16 per patient, not a change.
That gives ratios near 1, not changes.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: Patient 5's change is +70.2. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: A missing decimal point entered 79 instead of 7.9, so patient 5 seemed to rise by 70.2 points. Correcting the entry gives a fall of 0.9.
questions.takeaway: So: check every value is possible.
questions.hint_before_check: Which value is not a possible HbA1c?

code_note.title: Entry errors
code_note.text: R calculates with whatever values it is given.

science_note.title: Data entry checks
science_note.text: Trials check every value against a plausible range. HbA1c of 79% is impossible; one typo can change a whole result.

questions.scene_label: Patient 5's bar shoots off the card.

picture.description: Bars grow one after another against an optional reference line; value labels and a result note.
picture.label: HbA1c after the trial, per patient

b.feedback: That copies patient 5's before value, so their change becomes exactly 0: plausible, and wrong.
That divides every result by 10, not only the typo: all five become impossible.

c.feedback: rev() reverses before, so each patient is compared with someone else, and patient 5 is still wrong.
Rounding 79 leaves 79, so patient 5 still rises by 70.2.

That caps every change at 1, hiding the error instead of fixing it.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What is the average change?
questions.explanation_after_check: The five changes add to −3.2, and −3.2 / 5 = −0.64 points on average.
questions.takeaway: So: mean() summarises the whole trial.
questions.hint_before_check: mean() adds and divides by the count.

code_note.title: Summaries
code_note.text: R has functions that turn a vector into one number.

science_note.title: Average and individual
science_note.text: An average fall can hide a patient who got worse, like patient 2. Look at both.

questions.scene_label: The cards, with an average line to draw.

picture.description: Bars grow one after another against an optional reference line; value labels and a result note.
picture.label: HbA1c after the trial, per patient

questions.takeaway: So: divide by the starting value.
questions.hint_before_check: A percentage change is relative to what?

code_note.title: Percentages
code_note.text: A percentage change compares two values.

science_note.title: Reporting change
science_note.text: Trials report change against baseline. Using the wrong denominator overstates the benefit.

items.title: Length of stay
items.intro: Here are this week's five discharges from the medical ward, in days. Summarise their stays for the bed planning meeting.

recap.title: Stays summarised
recap.subtitle: 22 bed-days, an average of 4.4 days, and one stay recorded in hours fixed.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: How many bed-days did they use?
questions.explanation_after_check: sum() adds the stays: 3 + 5 + 2 + 8 + 4 = 22 bed-days.
questions.takeaway: So: sum() gives total bed-days.

code_note.title: Whole-vector functions
code_note.text: R has functions that work on a whole vector at once.

science_note.title: Bed-days
science_note.text: Bed-days count the beds used over time. They drive staffing and how many beds a ward needs.

questions.scene_label: Five patients, one row of day boxes each.

picture.label: Calendar rows for each patient and a bed-days display

options.feedback: That is the number of patients.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Find the average stay
questions.explanation_after_check: mean() adds the stays and divides by the number of patients: 22 / 5 = 4.4 days.
questions.takeaway: So: mean() gives the average stay.

code_note.title: Summaries
code_note.text: Several R functions summarise a vector in different ways.

science_note.title: Average length of stay
science_note.text: Average length of stay is one of the main measures hospitals compare between wards and over time.

questions.scene_label: The display, ready for the average.

picture.label: Calendar rows for each patient and a bed-days display

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The average comes out as 5.5. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: There are 5 patients, not 4, so dividing by 4 inflates the average. length(stays) counts them for you: 22 / 5 = 4.4.
questions.takeaway: So: let length() count the patients.

code_note.title: Counting with code
code_note.text: R can count values for you.

science_note.title: Hard-coded numbers
science_note.text: A patient count typed in by hand goes stale as soon as the list changes. Counting in code keeps it right.

questions.scene_label: An average with the wrong count.

picture.label: Calendar rows for each patient and a bed-days display

b.feedback: That always gives 1.
That still divides by 4: 5.5.

c.feedback: That undoes the 4 by hand on screen; avg itself stays wrong.
That rounds 5.5 to 6: still wrong.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: A 30-day stay is added. What is the average now?
questions.explanation_after_check: stays now has 6 values adding to 52, so the mean is 52 / 6 = 8.666667: one long stay nearly doubles the average.
questions.takeaway: So: one long stay shifts the average.
questions.next_bridge: fix a stay recorded in hours.
questions.hint_before_check: c() can add a value to an existing vector.

code_note.title: Growing a vector
code_note.text: `c()` can also add a value to an existing vector.

science_note.title: Outliers
science_note.text: One long stay pulls the average up. That is why length of stay is often reported as a median as well.

questions.scene_label: A sixth patient with a long stay.

picture.label: Calendar rows for each patient and a bed-days display

options.feedback: The first line added the new stay.
That is the new total, not the average.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: Patient 5's stay came in hours. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: 96 hours is 4 days. Entered as 96, it made the average 22.8 days; converted, the average is back to 4.4.
questions.takeaway: So: put every value in the same unit.
questions.hint_before_check: How many hours make a day?

code_note.title: Units
code_note.text: R does not know units.

science_note.title: Mixed systems
science_note.text: Emergency departments often record hours and wards record days. Mixing them distorts every summary.

questions.scene_label: A stay recorded in hours, shown as 96 days.

picture.label: Calendar rows for each patient and a bed-days display

a.feedback: That turns hours into a much bigger number.
There are 24 hours in a day, not 60.

b.feedback: That divides by 6 for 5 patients.
That types in a wrong count.

That divides every stay by 24, not only the one in hours.

items.title: Vaccination coverage
items.intro: Measles vaccination in four districts. The target is 95% of eligible children. Which districts are short?

recap.title: Coverage worked out
recap.subtitle: Coverage per district, the overall figure, and how many more children each district needs.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: How many children were vaccinated in total?
questions.explanation_after_check: sum() adds the four districts: 16350 children.
questions.takeaway: So: sum() totals every district.

code_note.title: Totals
code_note.text: Whole-vector functions work on any vector.

science_note.title: Measles coverage
science_note.text: Measles spreads so readily that about 95% of children need two doses to stop outbreaks.

picture.label: Children vaccinated by district

options.feedback: That is the number of districts.
That is the average per district.

questions.ask: Show coverage to one decimal place
questions.explanation_after_check: round(pct, 1) keeps one decimal place for each district.
questions.takeaway: So: round(x, 1) keeps one decimal.

code_note.title: Tidying output

science_note.title: Reporting coverage
science_note.text: Coverage is usually reported to one decimal place, enough to compare with a target.

questions.takeaway: So: divide, then multiply by 100.
questions.hint_before_check: What do the brackets divide by?

code_note.title: Combining districts
code_note.text: There is more than one way to combine rates.

science_note.title: Weighted figures
science_note.text: An overall rate should use total counts. Averaging rates gives small districts too much say.

science_note.text: Knowing how many children each district needs lets teams plan catch-up clinics where the gaps are.

items.title: Screening test
items.intro: 1000 people had a new bowel screening test, then a colonoscopy to confirm. Work out how good the test is.

recap.title: Test assessed
recap.subtitle: Sensitivity 0.9, specificity 0.905, and a positive predictive value of only 0.33.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: How many people had the disease?
questions.explanation_after_check: Everyone with the disease either tested positive (45) or was missed (5): 50.
questions.takeaway: So: everyone with the disease is tp + fn.

code_note.title: Building on arithmetic
code_note.text: Values combine with `+` as before.

science_note.title: The 2 by 2 table
science_note.text: Comparing a test with a definite diagnosis sorts people into true and false positives and negatives.

questions.scene_label: The screening grid: disease rows and test columns.

picture.description: A 2×2 screening grid whose cells light as the code reads them.
picture.label: Screening 2 by 2 grid with a result display

options.feedback: That adds the positive tests, true and false.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Work out the sensitivity
questions.explanation_after_check: Sensitivity is true positives out of everyone with the disease: 45 / 50 = 0.9.
questions.takeaway: So: sensitivity = tp / (tp + fn).
questions.hint_before_check: Of everyone with the disease, how many tested positive?

code_note.title: Ratios
code_note.text: The bottom of a fraction can be a sum.

science_note.title: Sensitivity
science_note.text: Sensitivity is how many people with the disease the test catches. Screening tests need it high.

questions.scene_label: The grid with the disease row lit.

picture.description: A 2×2 screening grid whose cells light as the code reads them.
picture.label: Screening 2 by 2 grid with a result display

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: Specificity comes out as 0.95. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: Specificity is true negatives out of everyone without the disease: 860 / (860 + 90) = 0.905.
questions.takeaway: So: specificity = tn / (tn + fp).
questions.next_bridge: work out the positive predictive value.
questions.hint_before_check: Specificity is about people without the disease.

code_note.title: The right group
code_note.text: Each rate is about one group of people.

science_note.title: Specificity
science_note.text: Specificity is how many people without the disease the test clears. Low specificity means many false alarms.

questions.scene_label: The grid with the no-disease row to light.

picture.description: A 2×2 screening grid whose cells light as the code reads them.
picture.label: Screening 2 by 2 grid with a result display

c.feedback: fn are people with the disease; specificity is about people without it.
That is the false positive rate, the opposite.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: If the test is positive, how likely is the disease?
questions.explanation_after_check: Of 135 positive tests, only 45 are true: 0.33. Even a good test gives many false alarms when the disease is rare.
questions.takeaway: So: PPV asks how many positives are real.
questions.hint_before_check: Of all positive tests, how many are true?

code_note.title: Different questions
code_note.text: The same counts answer different questions.

science_note.title: Predictive value
science_note.text: Patients ask "do I have it?", which is the positive predictive value, not the sensitivity.

picture.description: A 2×2 screening grid whose cells light as the code reads them.
picture.label: Screening 2 by 2 grid with a result display

options.feedback: That is the sensitivity, a different question.
That is how common the disease is.

questions.takeaway: So: bracket the sum before dividing.

code_note.title: Order of operations
code_note.text: R has rules for which operation comes first.

science_note.title: Prevalence
science_note.text: How common the disease is changes how useful a positive result is: rarer disease, more false alarms.

picture.label: Screening 2 by 2 grid with a result display
